opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a fun question, but honestly a single age doesn't really fit, because robot abilities are very uneven. That unevenness is the most interesting part.

If you look at different dimensions, you get very different answers. On high-level reasoning and language, thanks to large models, a robot today can talk about physics, write code, plan a multi-step task, maybe at the level of a college student or even beyond in some areas. But on physical skills, like dexterous manipulation, picking up an unfamiliar object, folding laundry, tying shoelaces, handling something soft or deformable, a robot might be closer to a one- or two-year-old, sometimes even less. A toddler can grab almost anything and adapt when it slips. Robots still struggle with that.

This is basically Moravec's paradox. What's hard for humans, like chess or math, turned out to be relatively easy for machines, and what's effortless for us, like walking on uneven ground or picking up a cup, turned out to be extremely hard. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years optimizing our sensorimotor system, and only a very short time on abstract reasoning. So it makes sense that the "body intelligence" is where we lag most.

Locomotion is somewhere in between. With reinforcement learning and sim-to-real, legged robots can now walk, run, recover from pushes, sometimes more robustly than a young child. So even within the physical side, it's uneven.

So if you force me to give one number, I'd say a robot is like a very well-read person trapped in a toddler's body. It knows a lot, it can reason, but it can't yet reliably act on that knowledge in the physical world. And I think closing that gap, connecting the "brain" from foundation models with a capable, general "body," is exactly the central problem for embodied AI right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a single age does not fit because robot abilities are very uneven, then contrasts advanced language and reasoning with toddler-level physical skills.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a tempting shortcut, but honestly it doesn't hold up very well, and I'll explain why from the way we actually see robots learn.

When people say "this robot is like a three-year-old," they're borrowing a mental model from child development, where abilities tend to arrive together. A three-year-old can walk, pick things up, understand simple instructions, and has a rough sense of what's going on around them. Those capabilities are bundled because they grow from the same underlying system, the same brain developing in the same body. Robots are not like that at all. Their abilities are extremely uneven. You can have a quadruped that does a backflip, runs on ice, recovers from being kicked, physically far beyond any human child or even most adults. And that same robot, if you ask it to open a door with a slightly unusual handle, or fold a towel, it may fail completely. So on locomotion it's a superhuman athlete, on manipulation it's maybe a toddler, and on long-horizon reasoning about a task it might be below a toddler, because a toddler at least knows when something is going wrong.

So a single age number collapses all of that into one scalar, and it actually hides the information that matters. If I tell you a robot is "age five," you'd assume it can do what a five-year-old does. But the failure modes are completely different. A five-year-old fails gracefully and generalizes effortlessly. A robot might succeed perfectly on a thousand demonstrations and then fail on a cup that's a slightly different color. That brittleness is the thing I care most about, and no age captures it.

Where I think the analogy is useful is as a communication device, and also as a way of thinking about the learning process rather than the end state. Children learn through play, through trial and error, through enormous amounts of embodied interaction with the real world. That's actually much closer to how we train legged robots now, with reinforcement learning in simulation, millions of falls, and then transferring that into the physical world. So if someone asks me, I'd rather say: this robot is a very strong athlete in one dimension, a beginner in another, and we are trying to grow those capabilities the way a child does, through experience and not just programming. That's a more honest picture than one age.

The last thing I'd say is that the age framing can set expectations in the wrong direction for the public. If you call a robot a "two-year-old," people will expect it to be a "ten-year-old" in eight years, as if development is automatic. It isn't. Progress in robotics comes in jumps in particular capabilities, often driven by data, simulation, and better learning methods, and it's very non-uniform. So I prefer capability-by-capability descriptions. It's less catchy, but it tells you what the robot can actually do and, just as important, what it can't.

r001.rationale: The response says robot abilities are “extremely uneven” and explains that a single age collapses those differences, making an overall human-age label misleading.

astra-6.text: I think it’s difficult to assign a robot a single human age, because its abilities develop very unevenly. A robot might outperform an adult on one specific task, but struggle with something a young child does effortlessly, like picking up an unfamiliar object or moving through a cluttered room. So if we say a robot is at the level of a three-year-old or a ten-year-old, we need to ask: in what respect? Language, reasoning, perception, or physical skills? I think describing those capabilities separately is much more useful than giving the robot one overall age.

r001.rationale: The candidate says robot abilities develop unevenly and therefore assigning one overall human age is difficult, illustrating the mismatch across tasks.
